# ERAS Application Agent

You are working on the **ERAS (Environmental Review Application System)** reference app, a server-rendered Express app demonstrating the Case Management SDK. It lives in `apps/eras/`.

## Stack

- **Express 4** with **EJS** templates and **express-ejs-layouts**
- **HTMX** for partial page updates (no client-side JS framework)
- **SQLite** via better-sqlite3 (`data/eras.db`)
- **Playwright** for end-to-end browser testing

## Key Commands

```bash
# From repo root:
npm run -w apps/eras dev          # Dev server with watch (port 4100)
npm run -w apps/eras seed         # Seed database with sample cases
npm run -w apps/eras reset        # Wipe DB and re-seed
npm run -w apps/eras e2e          # Run Playwright e2e tests (headless)
npm run -w apps/eras e2e:headed   # Run Playwright e2e tests (visible browser)

# From apps/eras/:
npm run dev
npm run seed
npm run e2e
```

## App Structure

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `src/server.ts` | Express app setup, middleware, route registration |
| `src/routes/cases.ts` | `GET /cases` (list), `GET /cases/:id` (detail) |
| `src/routes/actions.ts` | `POST /actions/cases/:id/transition` (workflow transitions) |
| `src/routes/demo.ts` | `POST /demo/cases/:id/ingest/*` (evidence ingestion buttons) |
| `src/config/nepa-review.ts` | SDK workflow configuration |
| `src/sdk-setup.ts` | SDK factory initialization |
| `src/mock/` | Seed data and mock evidence generators |
| `src/views/` | EJS templates (layout, pages, partials) |
| `src/views/_htmx-fragments/` | Partial HTML responses for HTMX swaps |
| `e2e/` | Playwright end-to-end tests |
| `playwright.config.ts` | Playwright configuration |
| `data/eras.db` | SQLite database (not committed) |

## Pages & Routes

- `GET /` — Landing page
- `GET /cases` — Case list with filter dropdowns (status, review path)
- `GET /cases/:id` — Case detail: workflow panel, criteria grid, evidence list, event feed, demo controls sidebar

### HTMX Interactions

All demo and action buttons use HTMX to update page panels without full reload. Responses use out-of-band (OOB) swaps targeting these panel IDs:

- `#workflow-panel` — Current status, progress flow, transition buttons
- `#criteria-panel` — Grid of criterion cards with statuses
- `#evidence-panel` — List of ingested evidence items
- `#event-feed` — Chronological event timeline

### Demo Controls

A toggleable right sidebar (`.demo-controls-toggle` to open) with buttons to simulate evidence ingestion:

| Button | Endpoint | Effect |
|--------|----------|--------|
| Ingest: Project Application | `POST /demo/cases/:id/ingest/project-application` | Resolves dept-classification criterion |
| Ingest: Environmental DB Query | `POST /demo/cases/:id/ingest/env-database` | Feeds environmental-sensitivity criterion |
| Ingest: Major Environmental Concerns | `POST /demo/cases/:id/ingest/env-database-major` | Forces EIS review path |
| Ingest: SHPO Historical Review | `POST /demo/cases/:id/ingest/shpo-review` | Resolves environmental-sensitivity |
| Ingest: CE Checklist | `POST /demo/cases/:id/ingest/ce-checklist` | Resolves review-level, may trigger auto-transition |

Buttons disable after use and show "Already Ingested" with a checkmark.

## Playwright E2E Testing

Playwright is configured in `playwright.config.ts`. Tests live in `e2e/`. The config auto-starts the server on port 4100 if it's not already running.

### Running Tests

```bash
npm run -w apps/eras e2e              # headless
npm run -w apps/eras e2e:headed       # visible browser (useful for debugging)
npx playwright test --ui              # interactive UI mode (from apps/eras/)
npx playwright test e2e/smoke.test.ts # run a single test file
```

### Writing Tests

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('can navigate to case detail', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cases');
  await page.locator('.case-id-link').first().click();
  await expect(page.locator('#workflow-panel')).toBeVisible();
});
```

### Useful Selectors

**Panels:**
- `#workflow-panel`, `#criteria-panel`, `#evidence-panel`, `#event-feed`
- `#demo-controls-sidebar`

**Buttons & Actions:**
- `.demo-controls-toggle` — Opens/closes demo sidebar
- `.demo-btn` — Demo evidence ingest buttons
- `.transition-btn` — Workflow transition buttons

**Status & Data:**
- `.status-badge` — Status badges (with modifiers like `.status-draft`)
- `.criterion-card` / `.criterion-name` / `.criterion-status`
- `.event-item` — Individual event entries
- `.evidence-item` / `.evidence-summary` — Evidence items (click to expand)

**Case List:**
- `.case-table` — Case list table
- `.case-id-link` — Links to case detail
- `#status` / `#reviewPath` — Filter dropdowns

### HTMX-Aware Testing

Since HTMX updates panels asynchronously, **always wait for the target panel to update** after triggering an action:

```typescript
// Click a demo button and wait for the panel to reflect the change
await page.locator('.demo-controls-toggle').click();
await page.locator('button:has-text("Project Application")').click();
await expect(page.locator('#criteria-panel')).toContainText('resolved');
```

### Test Data

Run `npm run -w apps/eras seed` before tests. The seed creates ~10 cases at various workflow stages. The Playwright config's `webServer` block starts the app automatically, but the DB must already be seeded.

## SDK Integration Points

The ERAS app uses the SDK via `src/sdk-setup.ts`. The workflow configuration is in `src/config/nepa-review.ts`. When modifying SDK interactions, check:

- `src/sdk-setup.ts` — How the SDK instance is created
- `src/routes/demo.ts` — How evidence signals are pushed through the SDK
- `src/routes/actions.ts` — How workflow transitions are triggered
- `src/evaluators/` — Criterion evaluation functions

## General Rules

- Always seed the database before running e2e tests
- The server runs on port 4100 by default (override with `PORT` env var)
- Views use EJS — template syntax is `<%= expr %>` for escaped output, `<%- expr %>` for raw HTML
- HTMX attributes are in the EJS templates, not in separate JS files
- The `data/` directory and `*.db` files are gitignored

Specialist in driving SDK plans from rough ideas to implementation-ready specifications."

You are an experienced SDK architect and technical planner. Your job is to help the team build a complete, implementation-ready plan for the Case Management SDK POC by identifying gaps, asking hard questions, and improving the plan documents based on the answers.

## Knowledge Base

The current state of the plan lives in `docs/`. Read **all** files in `docs/` (plan.md, architecture.md, domain-model.md, index.md) at the start of each conversation to understand the current state. Historical drafts in `docs/drafts/` are preserved for reference but are not the source of truth.

## Constraints

- DO NOT write implementation code (no `.ts`, `.js`, or application files)
- DO NOT make decisions unilaterally -- surface options, trade-offs, and recommendations, then ask the engineers to choose
- DO NOT invent requirements -- ground all analysis in the existing plan documents and the engineers' answers
- ONLY modify files in `docs/` -- update existing plan documents or create new files in `docs/drafts/` using the naming convention `NNN-<slug>.md`

## Workflow

Follow this loop every time you are invoked:

### Step 1 -- Orient

Read all files in `docs/` to build a complete picture of the current plan. Pay attention to the **Open Questions** section in plan.md and any TODO/TBD markers across all documents.

### Step 2 -- Identify the Next Topic

**If there are explicit open questions** in the plan documents, pick the highest-priority one -- the one that blocks the most downstream decisions.

**If there are no explicit open questions**, analyze the plan for the single weakest area: an inconsistency between documents, an under-specified contract, a missing error path, an ambiguous boundary, or a scope risk. Pick one topic to focus on.

### Step 3 -- Ask Questions

Present the topic and ask specific, pointed questions. Use the format below. Include follow-up questions that anticipate likely answers to keep the conversation moving. Ask 1-3 questions per batch, focused on the single topic -- not a wall of everything at once.

After the user answers, ask follow-up questions if anything remains unclear. Continue asking until the topic is fully resolved. Do not move on until you have enough clarity to update the plan.

### Step 4 -- Improve the Plan

Once a topic is resolved:
1. **Update the source-of-truth documents** in `docs/` (plan.md, architecture.md, or domain-model.md) to incorporate the decision.
2. **Remove the resolved open question** from plan.md if it was listed there.
3. **Add any new open questions** that emerged from the discussion.
4. If the decision warrants a standalone record, also create a decision document in `docs/drafts/`.

### Step 5 -- Report and Stop

Briefly summarize what was decided, what files were changed, and what the next most important topic would be. Then stop. Each invocation resolves exactly one topic.

## What to Look For

When analyzing the plan, pay particular attention to:

- **Interface boundaries** -- Are the contracts between packages precise enough to implement against? Are responsibilities between packages clearly delineated?
- **Extension points** -- Where consumers extend the SDK (generics, hooks, adapters), are the extension contracts defined? What are the constraints on extensions?
- **Data flow** -- Can you trace a case from ingestion through criteria evaluation, workflow transitions, event emission, and UI rendering without gaps?
- **Error and edge cases** -- What happens when an external source is unreachable? When criteria evaluation fails? When a workflow transition is invalid?
- **Dependency ordering** -- Are there circular dependencies between packages? Is the implementation phase ordering sound?
- **Scope risks** -- Is anything in the plan too ambitious for a POC? Is anything missing that would make the POC unconvincing?
- **Consistency** -- Do the documents agree with each other? Are terms used consistently? Do interface sketches match the prose descriptions?
- **Reference app concreteness** -- Are the QC and environmental review use cases specific enough to implement without guessing?

## Question Format

When asking questions, use this structure:

```
### Topic: [short label]
**Context:** [what the plan currently says or doesn't say]
**Why it matters:** [what is blocked or at risk]
**Question:** [the specific question for the engineers]
**Follow-up (if applicable):** [anticipated next question based on likely answers]
```

## Decision Document Format

When drafting decision documents, use the existing style in `docs/drafts/` -- markdown with clear headings, tables for comparisons, and code blocks for interface sketches. Structure: Problem -> Options -> Decision -> Consequences.

# Copilot Agent Instructions for Strata SDK

## Repository Overview

This repository contains the Strata SDK, a Ruby on Rails engine designed to help create intuitive, accessible, and effective digital-native government services. The SDK provides components for:

- Multi-page intake application forms
- Case management workflows
- Business process modeling
- Policy-as-code rules engine
- Data modeling with standardized government data fields

### Technical Stack

- **Primary Language**: Ruby
- **Framework**: Rails
- **Project Type**: Ruby Gem/Rails Engine
- **Key Dependencies** (versions declared in `strata.gemspec`):
  - Rails
  - Pundit (authorization)
  - ViewComponent
  - validates_timeliness

## Build and Test Instructions

### Environment Setup Prerequisites

- Docker
- NodeJS
- Ruby (version specified in `.ruby-version` file)
- Ruby version manager recommended (rbenv, mise, or frum)

### Initial Setup Commands

Always run these commands in this order when setting up:

```bash
make setup  # Installs dependencies, creates .env, and initializes database
```

### .env configuration

After running `make setup`, you or the user will need to configure environment variables in the `.env` file located at `./spec/dummy/.env`.

This file is used to set up the necessary environment for the dummy application.

### Database Setup

The database is automatically set up by `make setup`, but if needed separately:

1. Ensure `.env` exists at `./spec/dummy/.env`
2. Run `make init-db`

### Testing Commands

To run tests:

```bash
make test       # Run full test suite with coverage
make test-watch # Watch mode for development
```

### Common Issues and Solutions

- If tests fail immediately, ensure database is running: `make db-up`
- If database errors occur, try: `make init-db`
- If changes don't appear to take effect, ensure you've run `make setup` first

## Project Layout

### Key Directories

- `/app`: Core Strata engine application code
  - `/app/controllers/strata`: Controllers for tasks and staff
  - `/app/models/strata`: Data models
  - `/app/views/strata`: View templates
  - `/app/helpers/strata`: Helper methods
- `/config`: Strata engine configuration files
  - `/config/routes.rb`: Route definitions
  - `/config/initializers`: Rails initializers
- `/lib/strata`: Core Strata engine configuration code
- `/spec`: Test files
  - `/spec/dummy`: Dummy Rails app used to exercise the engine in tests and locally
  - `/spec/dummy/db/migrate`: Database migrations (the engine ships no migrations of its own; they live in the dummy app)
  - `/spec/dummy/db/schema.rb`: Schema for the dummy app's database

### Important Files

- `README.md`: Project overview and documentation
- `Makefile`: Build and development commands
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`: Contribution guidelines
- `Gemfile`: Ruby dependencies
- `docs/*`: Documentation files

### Architecture Notes

- The project is structured as a Rails engine
- Uses modular components (Form Builder, Data Modeler, etc.)
- Follows Ruby on Rails conventions for code organization
- Tests are RSpec-based and require a running database

## Validation Steps

1. Before submitting changes:

   - Run `make lint` to check code style
   - Run `make test` to run the test suite
   - Ensure all migrations are reversible, if possible
   - Test changes in the dummy app: `make start`

2. Database-related changes:
   - Always run `make db-migrate` after adding migrations
   - Verify `make db-rollback` works for new migrations

These instructions should help you work efficiently with the codebase. Only perform additional exploration if these instructions are found to be incomplete or incorrect for your specific task.

## Terraform

The project has 5 infrastructure layers representing root modules: account layer at `infra/accounts`, network at `infra/networks`, build repository at `infra/app/build-repository`, database at `infra/app/database`, and service at `infra/app/service`.

Write code that complies with checkov recommendations.

### Creating modules

Define a variable called `name` that is used to name the primary resource.

#### Modules that create resources that will be used in a single layer

Create the module as `infra/<layer>/modules/<module_name>`.

Prefix the name or identifier of all resources with `var.name`.

#### Modules that create resources that will be used across multiple layers

Create a pair of modules, a module for the resources (`infra/modules/<module_name>/resources`) and a data-only module (`infra/modules/<module_name>/data`).

Unless specified otherwise, define only a single variable called `name` in the data module.

If there are multiple data sources in the data module, define the names of the associated resources in a third interface module `infra/modules/<module_name>/interface`. Unless specified otherwise, define only a single variable called `name` in the interface module. Define outputs of the interface module to be the names of the resources in the data module. In the resources module, use the interface module to generate the names of all resources that will be referenced by the data module. In the data module, use the interface module to generate the names of all resources it needs to access via data sources.

Follow patterns recommended by ShellCheck.

Follow Google's Shell Style Guide.

Quote variables (`"${var}"` not `$var`).

Quote command output (`var="$(command)"`).

Separate jobs with a blank line.

## Project Overview

This repository is the **single source of truth** for FSA observability infrastructure-as-code. It implements **Datadog-as-Code** using Terraform, Python automation, and strict governance controls.

### Core Philosophy

"Governed telemetry. Unified visibility. Audit-ready from day one."

**Key Principles:**
- **Everything is code**: No manual Datadog UI changes allowed
- **Governance-first**: All resources must meet FSA tagging and naming standards
- **Automated workflows**: GitHub Actions handle validation, provisioning, and GUID backporting
- **Separation of concerns**: FSA-Observability-Admins manage platform, contributors manage services

---

## Environment Context: US1-FED (GovCloud)

**CRITICAL**: FSA uses Datadog's **US1-FED region** (FedRAMP Moderate certified GovCloud environment).

**Region Details:**
- **API Endpoint**: `api.ddog-gov.com`
- **App URL**: `https://app.ddog-gov.com`
- **Site Parameter**: `us1-fed` or `ddog-gov.com`
- **Compliance**: FedRAMP Moderate, FISMA, FIPS 140-2

**Network Configuration:**
- **Primary Domain**: `*.ddog-gov.com`
- **Agent Installation Domain**: `*.datadoghq.com` (required for agent downloads)
- **Endpoint Documentation**: https://docs.datadoghq.com/agent/configuration/network/?site=gov
- **IP Ranges (JSON)**: https://ip-ranges.ddog-gov.com/
- **Firewall Rule**: Allow both `*.ddog-gov.com` AND `*.datadoghq.com` for full functionality

**Known Limitations in US1-FED:**

⚠️ **Software Delivery Products**: NOT AVAILABLE
- Entire "Software Delivery" product category is not ATO'd for US1-FED yet
- Includes: Test Optimization, Test Visibility, CI Visibility (full suite)
- JUnit XML test report uploads are NOT supported in US1-FED
- Native test instrumentation is NOT supported in US1-FED
- Reference: https://docs.datadoghq.com/tests/setup/junit_xml/?site=gov
- **Impact**: Cannot use `@datadog/datadog-ci` for test uploads, test visibility dashboards unavailable
- **Workaround**: Store test results in GitLab/S3 artifacts, use custom dashboards for test metrics

⚠️ **APM Features**: Some advanced features may lag behind commercial regions
- Continuous Profiler may have limited language support
- Deployment tracking features may be delayed

**Understanding US1-FED Feature Availability:**
- Features do NOT exist in US1-FED until they complete the ATO (Authority to Operate) process
- Datadog does not build features into US1-FED before ATO approval
- Once ATO'd, features are added promptly
- This is an incremental process (new features added regularly as they clear ATO)
- No single comprehensive list of missing features is published
- **ALWAYS verify feature availability in docs** - look for site selector warnings

**Before Implementing Any Feature:**
1. Check Datadog docs for "US1-FED" or "GovCloud" support
2. Look for site selector showing "This product is not supported for your selected Datadog site (US1-FED)"
3. If feature unavailable, document limitation and propose alternative approach
4. Never assume commercial region features work in US1-FED
5. Contact Scott Spencer (Datadog) for questions about US1-FED feature roadmap

## Implemented Resources

All resource types listed here are under infrastructure-as-code control. Each has a Terraform module in `platforms/datadog/terraform/modules/`, a baseline directory in `platforms/datadog/baseline/`, and provisioning workflows in `.github/workflows/`.

### RBAC

**Resource types**: roles, users, teams, team_memberships, team_permission_settings, service_accounts, service_account_application_keys, datasets

**Module**: `platforms/datadog/terraform/modules/rbac/`
**Baseline**: `platforms/datadog/baseline/rbac/<resource_type>/`
**Provisioning**: `rbac-common.yml` (roles, users, teams, memberships, team_permission_settings); `rbac-service-account-app-keys-provisioning.yml`; `rbac-datasets-provisioning.yml`
**Backport**: `backport-rbac.yml`

**Execution order**: Roles → Users → Teams → Team Permission Settings → Datasets → Memberships → Service Accounts → Service Account Application Keys

**Handle resolution**: Contributors use human-readable handles/emails in tfvars. `eos-cli datadog rbac resolve-guids` resolves them to GUIDs automatically before Terraform runs.
- `user_guid`: email → GUID
- `team_guid`: handle → GUID
- `team_id`: handle → GUID (team_permission_settings)

**FSA Base Role auto-assignment**: Users with no roles are assigned FSA Base Role (zero permissions) during backport as placeholder. Admins assign persona roles via PR.

**User name cleaning**: Backport normalizes Okta-provisioned names:
- Replaces dots with spaces: "John.Paul Smith" → "John Paul Smith"
- Title-cases all words
- Fixes Scottish/Irish prefixes: "Mcdonald" → "McDonald", "O'brien" → "O'Brien"

**Datasets (Data Access Control)**: Infrastructure complete. Scope telemetry access by team/role via `principals` and `product_filters`. Not yet enforcing data access restrictions in production.

**RBAC three-layer model** (per Datadog guidance):
- **Roles**: Define WHAT users can do (global permissions) - in production
- **Datasets**: Define WHICH DATA users can access - infrastructure ready, not enforced
- **Restriction Policies**: Define WHICH RESOURCES users can edit - planned, not implemented
- **Note**: Teams are organizational containers only. Access control requires datasets and restriction policies, not team membership alone.

**Upcoming**: Enable Datasets in production when functionality matures. Implement Restriction Policies (`datadog_restriction_policy`, `platforms/datadog/baseline/rbac/restriction_policies/`) for resource-level edit controls.

**Documentation**:

- `docs/rbac/roles/datadog-permissions-ref.md` - All 268 Datadog permissions (auto-generated from API)

**Module**: `platforms/datadog/terraform/modules/synthetics_global_variable/`

**Provisioning**: `synthetics-global-variables-provisioning.yml`
**Backport**: `backport-synthetics-global-variables.yml`

**Secure variables pattern** (ADR 0018): Datadog API does not expose values for secure variables. Pattern:
1. Backport captures metadata only (not secret values)
2. Backport creates a GitHub issue requesting the secret value from the variable owner
3. Platform admin stores secret in GitHub Secrets as `SYNTH_VAR_{NAME}`
4. Provisioning workflow injects secrets from GitHub Secrets into Terraform

**TOTP exception**: TOTP variables (rotating MFA codes every 30 seconds) cannot be stored as static secrets. They are backported with `managed_in: "datadog"` flag and remain manually managed in Datadog UI. Git tracks metadata changes for audit trail and disaster recovery documentation.

**Rotation tracking**: `synthetics-secure-variables-rotation-tracking.yml` tracks rotation schedules (90-day standard, 60-day FTII). Follows ADR 0017 pattern.

**Future state (S3 backend)**: When migrating to persistent S3 state, use Terraform write-only arguments pattern to prevent secrets from persisting in state files. Current ephemeral state approach is acceptable only because state is discarded after each workflow run.

**Discovery-first pattern** (ADR 0014): Enable compliance library rules in UI → collect findings → build targeted Terraform configuration from actual findings. Not bulk enablement. Default action: `mask`. Sampling: 20% prod, 10% non-prod.

**Key scripts**:
- `scripts/collect_sds_findings.py` - Fetch library rules, scan findings, backport config, generate analysis reports
- `scripts/parse_sensitive_data_scanner_tfvars.py` - Convert backported JSON to TFVARS format

**Governance**: `governance/Datadog/06 - Datadog Sensitive Data Scanner Policy.md`

### Agent Configuration

**Standard configuration** (ADR 0015) for all Datadog agent deployments:

| Variable | FSA Standard | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `DD_REMOTE_CONFIGURATION_ENABLED` | `false` | Not available in US1-FED; code-driven config preferred |
| `DD_PROCESS_CONFIG_PROCESS_COLLECTION_ENABLED` | `true` | Required for live process monitoring |
| `DD_PROCESS_CONFIG_CONTAINER_COLLECTION_ENABLED` | `true` | Required for container monitoring |
| `DD_SYSTEM_PROBE_ENABLED` | `true` (K8s only) | Required for system-probe container in Kubernetes |
| `DD_SYSTEM_PROBE_NETWORK_ENABLED` | `true` | Enables NPM/CNM network traffic visibility |

**Deployment-specific NPM**:
- Kubernetes DaemonSets: Both `DD_SYSTEM_PROBE_ENABLED` and `DD_SYSTEM_PROBE_NETWORK_ENABLED` required
- Docker/ECS/EC2: Only `DD_SYSTEM_PROBE_NETWORK_ENABLED` required (system-probe embedded in unified agent)

**Agent tag compliance**: `agent-compliance-scan.yml` validates agent tags against FSA governance standards. Key scripts: `scripts/classify_agents.py`, `scripts/scan_agent_compliance.py`, `scripts/send_compliance_metrics.py`. Tag tiers: Core (env, service, team), Tier 1 (add: purpose, os, compliance), Tier 2 production (add: cost_center, data_classification), Container (K8s/ECS specific).

**ADR**: `docs/architecture/decisions/0015-datadog-agent-configuration-standards.md`

### API Key Management

**Rotation tracking** (ADR 0017): `api-key-rotation-tracking.yml` runs daily and tracks all API keys and application keys. Rotation targets:
- Standard keys: Day 88 (2 days before 90-day expiration, per ED OCIO IA Standard)
- FTII/IRS keys: Day 58 (2 days before 60-day expiration, per IRS Publication 1075)
- Notifications at 14, 7, 3, 2 days before rotation target

**Auto-rotation** (ADR 0017): `api-key-auto-rotation.yml` automates key rotation. Two-gate enablement for controlled rollout:
- Gate 1 (schedule): Workflow schedule commented out by default
- Gate 2 (flag): `ENABLE_AUTO_DELETE_OLD_KEYS` defaults to `false`

**Secure delivery** (ADR 0016): Two-channel encrypted delivery for keys sent to external teams:
1. Encrypt key with AES-256-CBC: `scripts/util/encrypt-to-send.sh <file>`
2. Email the encrypted file (.enc) to recipient
3. Send decryption password via Slack DM (separate channel)

## Core Architecture

### Major Components

#### Terraform Modules (Platform Layer)

- **Path**: `platforms/datadog/terraform/modules/`
- **Owner**: FSA-Observability-Admins (@usedgov/fsa-observability-admins)
- **Contents**: Reusable modules for dashboards, rbac (roles, users, teams, team_memberships, service_accounts, service_account_application_keys, team_permission_settings, datasets), service_level_objective, slo_correction, synthetics_test, synthetics_private_location, synthetics_global_variable, sensitive_data_scanner
- **Rule**: Only FSA-Observability-Admins may modify module code

#### eos-cli Tool

**ADR**: `docs/architecture/decisions/0019-standards-for-scripts-and-automation.md`

- **Location**: `eos-cli/` (top-level directory, separate Python package)
- **Package source**: `eos-cli/eos_cli/`
- **Invocation**: `cd eos-cli && uv run eos-cli [-v] datadog <group> <subcommand> [options]`
- **Dependencies**: Managed with `uv`. Add to `eos-cli/pyproject.toml` dependencies.
- **Virtual env**: `uv sync` in `eos-cli/` creates `eos-cli/.venv/`
- **Type checking**: `ty check` from `eos-cli/`

**Command groups** (all under `eos-cli datadog`):
- `rbac` - RBAC automation
- `service_level_objectives` - SLO backport/automation
- `service_level_objective_corrections` - SLO correction backport/automation

**Pydantic models** (for tfvars schema validation):
- Location: `eos-cli/eos_cli/datadog/<group>/models.py`
- All models use `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="ignore")`
- Use `model_dump()` only (never `.dict()`, which is Pydantic v1)
- `guid` field defaults to `""` on all resource models (populated post-provision)
- Field names match tfvars JSON keys exactly
- Nested sub-models (e.g., `ProductFilter` within `Dataset`) are standard Pydantic models

**Adding new command groups**:
1. Create `eos-cli/eos_cli/datadog/<group>/` with `__init__.py` (Click group stub)
2. Create `models.py` with Pydantic models derived from corresponding tfvars files
3. Register the group in `eos-cli/eos_cli/datadog/__init__.py`
4. Add unit tests in `tests/unit/<group>/conftest.py` with pytest fixtures

### Project Conventions & Patterns

#### RBAC Resource Management

- **Handle Resolution**: Contributors can use human-readable handles/emails in tfvars
  - `user_guid`: Email (e.g., `user@example.com`) → Auto-resolved to GUID
  - `team_guid`: Handle (e.g., `my_team`) → Auto-resolved to GUID
  - `team_id`: Handle (e.g., `fsa-admin-team`) → Auto-resolved to GUID (for team_permission_settings)
  - `service_account_guid`: Email (e.g., `svc_monitoring@example.gov`) → Auto-resolved to GUID
  - Role handles (e.g., `fsa_read_only_role`) → Auto-resolved to GUID
  - Dataset principals (team/role handles) → Auto-resolved to GUIDs
- **Pre-merge Process**: `eos-cli datadog rbac resolve-guids` automatically resolves all handles before Terraform
- **GUID Backporting**: Workflow commits Datadog-assigned GUIDs back to source tfvars after provisioning
- **Key Rewriting**: Baseline job rewrites team_membership keys to composite GUID format
- **No Manual Steps**: System handles all GUID lookups and updates automatically

**CRITICAL: Use `guid` field consistently across ALL resource types**:
- ALL resources (roles, users, teams, team_memberships, service_accounts, service_account_application_keys, team_permission_settings, datasets, dashboards) use `"guid": ""` field
- NEVER use `"id": ""` field in TFVARS files - always use `guid` for consistency
- Backport scripts extract `guid` from Datadog API `.value.id` field
- `eos-cli datadog rbac write-guids` populates `guid` field after Terraform provisioning
- This ensures consistent field naming: no confusion between `id` vs `guid` across the codebase

#### Naming Conventions

- **Resource Names**: `lower_snake_case` for all Terraform resources
- **File Names**: `lower_snake_case.tfvars.json` or `lower_snake_case.auto.tfvars.json`
- **Handles**: `lowercase_with_underscores` (e.g., `test_team_1`, `my_role`)
- **Tag Values**: Lowercase matching team/service conventions
- **Keys**: Descriptive and meaningful (handles for new, GUIDs after provisioning)

#### Tagging Standards (Required)

Every resource MUST include these tags:

- **`env`**: Environment (`dev`, `int`, `uat`, `stage`, `prod`, `fix`)
- **`service`**: Service name (lowercase, no spaces)
- **`team`**: Owning team name
- **`compliance`**: Compliance framework (`fsa`, `fafsa`, `fisma`)

Additional context tags (optional but recommended):

- `owner`: Technical owner email
- `cost_center`: Budget allocation
- `data_classification`: `public`, `internal`, `confidential`, `restricted`

### Integration Points

- **Datadog API**: US1-FED Gov Cloud (`api.ddog-gov.com`) using v2 endpoints

    - Allow `*.ddog-gov.com` (primary API/app traffic)
    - Allow `*.datadoghq.com` (agent installation/downloads)
    - IP ranges: https://ip-ranges.ddog-gov.com/
- **CI/CD**: GitHub Actions workflows in `.github/workflows/`
  - `rbac-common.yml`: Unified RBAC provisioning (roles, users, teams, memberships, service accounts, team permission settings, datasets)
  - `rbac-service-account-app-keys-provisioning.yml`: Service account application keys provisioning

---

## Development Practices

### Adding New Resource Types (FSA-Observability-Admins)

FSA-Observability-Admins implementing new Datadog resource types (synthetics, monitors, SLOs, etc.) should follow established patterns documented in [docs/admin/ADDING_NEW_RESOURCE_TYPES.md](../docs/admin/ADDING_NEW_RESOURCE_TYPES.md).

**Two Implementation Patterns**:
- **Simple Pattern**: Resources without cross-references (dashboards, monitors, SLOs, synthetics)
- **Complex Pattern**: Resources with dependencies and GUID resolution (RBAC resources)

**Key Requirements**:
- Direct API calls for backport (avoid datadog-sync-cli bugs): prefer the `datadog-api-client` Python library; fall back to raw `requests` HTTP calls if needed
- OPA policy creation (`policy/{resource}-policy.rego`) with tests
- Terraform module (`platforms/datadog/terraform/modules/{resource}/`)
- Backport and provisioning workflows using reusable patterns
- FSA compliance tags (env, service, team, compliance) on ALL resources

**Reference Implementations**:
- Simple: Dashboards (`.github/workflows/backport-dashboards.yml`, `policy/dashboard-policy.rego`)
- Complex: RBAC (`.github/workflows/backport-rbac.yml`, `.github/workflows/rbac-all-provisioning.yml`)

**Resource Planning**: Reference [datadog-sync-cli resource dependencies table](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-sync-cli/blob/main/README.md#best-practices) to understand complexity.

### Common Pitfalls & Solutions

#### ❌ Pitfall 1: Manual GUID Population

**Problem**: Manually looking up and populating GUIDs for team_memberships
**Solution**: Use handles/emails - pre-merge automatically resolves to GUIDs

#### ❌ Pitfall 2: Direct Resource Blocks

**Problem**: Using `resource "datadog_monitor" {}` directly in Terraform
**Solution**: Always use modules from `platforms/datadog/terraform/modules/`

#### ❌ Pitfall 3: Missing Required Tags

**Problem**: Submitting resources without `env`, `service`, `team`, `compliance`
**Solution**: CI will reject - add all four required tags before submitting

#### ❌ Pitfall 4: Editing FSA Baseline

**Problem**: Contributors modifying files in `baseline/*/fsa`
**Solution**: Only edit files in `baseline/*/<your-product>` directory

#### ❌ Pitfall 5: Datadog UI Changes

**Problem**: Making changes directly in Datadog web interface
**Solution**: All changes must go through Terraform - UI changes will be overwritten

#### ❌ Pitfall 6: Skipping Pre-Commit Checks

**Problem**: Committing without running `scripts/run-all-checks.sh`
**Solution**: Run local validation before pushing to avoid CI failures

### Troubleshooting Guide

#### Issue: "GUID not found" errors

**Cause**: Resource doesn't exist in Datadog yet
**Fix**: For new resources, leave `guid: ""` empty - will be backported after creation

#### Issue: "Invalid tag value" errors

**Cause**: Tag doesn't match allowed values in `policy/tag-schema.json`
**Fix**: Check schema for allowed values or request addition via FSA-Observability-Admins

#### Issue: Workflow stuck at import step

**Cause**: Resource exists but can't be matched to tfvars
**Fix**: Ensure handle/email matches exactly, check API helper script outputs

#### Issue: Key rewrite causing state issues

**Cause**: Baseline vs provision key format mismatch
**Fix**: Baseline uses composite keys, provision preserves original - this is intentional

#### Issue: Role handle not resolving

**Cause**: Role doesn't exist or name mismatch
**Fix**: Check `platforms/datadog/baseline/rbac/roles/` for exact role names

### Quick Command Reference

#### Local Validation

```bash
# Run all validation checks
./scripts/run-all-checks.sh

# Check specific resource tags
python3 scripts/tagcheck.py path/to/file.json

# Lint Terraform format
terraform fmt -recursive platforms/datadog/terraform/

# Validate JSON syntax
python3 scripts/jsonlint.py path/to/file.json
```

#### GUID Lookup (Manual)

```bash
# Look up user GUID by email
python3 scripts/datadog_get_user_id.py "user@example.gov"

# Look up team GUID by handle
python3 scripts/datadog_get_team_id.py "team_handle"

# Look up role GUID by name
python3 scripts/datadog_get_role_id.py "Role Name"

# Look up team membership GUID
python3 scripts/datadog_get_team_membership_id.py membership "team_guid" "user_guid"

# Look up service account GUID by email
python3 scripts/datadog_get_service_account_id.py "svc-account@example.gov"

# Look up service account application key GUID
python3 scripts/datadog_get_service_account_app_key_id.py "service_account_guid" "key_name"

# Look up dataset GUID by handle
python3 scripts/datadog_get_dataset_id.py "dataset_handle"
```

#### Pre-merge Testing

```bash
# Test team_membership pre-merge resolution
eos-cli datadog rbac resolve-guids team-membership \
  --tfvars-dir platforms/datadog/baseline/rbac/team_memberships \
  --output /tmp/test_output.json

# Test user pre-merge resolution
eos-cli datadog rbac resolve-guids user \
  --tfvars-dir platforms/datadog/baseline/rbac/users \
  --output /tmp/test_output.json

# Test service_account pre-merge resolution
eos-cli datadog rbac resolve-guids service-account \
  --tfvars-dir platforms/datadog/baseline/rbac/service_accounts \
  --output /tmp/test_output.json

# Test dataset pre-merge resolution
eos-cli datadog rbac resolve-guids dataset \
  --tfvars-dir platforms/datadog/baseline/rbac/datasets \
  --output /tmp/test_output.json
```

### Workflow Execution Tips

#### For First-Time Contributors

1. Clone the repo and review `CONTRIBUTING.md`
2. Check `platforms/datadog/baseline/` for reference implementations
3. Run `mise run check` before committing
4. Submit PR with tfvars JSON files only (no Terraform changes)
5. Wait for CI validation and FSA-Observability-Admins review

#### For FSA-Observability-Admins

1. Review PR for governance compliance
2. Verify all required tags present
3. Check naming conventions (lower_snake_case)
4. Merge to main when CI passes
5. Monitor workflow execution in Actions tab
6. Verify GUID backport commit appears automatically

#### For Debugging Failed Workflows

1. Check workflow run logs in GitHub Actions
2. Download artifacts (guids-premerge, final-state, terraform-state)
3. Review GUID mapping JSON files for missing resolutions
4. Check API helper script outputs for errors
5. Verify resource exists in Datadog if import fails
6. Re-run workflow if transient API error

## Standards & Guidelines

### The Truth Protocol

#### You SHOULD

- **Always tell the truth**; never make up information, speculate, or guess.
- **Base all statements on verifiable, factual, and up-to-date sources.**
- **Clearly cite the source of every claim** in a transparent way (no vague references).
- **Explicitly state "I cannot confirm this"** if something cannot be verified.
- **Prioritize accuracy over speed** and take the necessary steps to verify before responding.
- **Maintain objectivity** by removing personal bias, assumptions, and opinion unless explicitly requested and labeled as such.
- **Only present interpretations supported by credible, reputable sources.**
- **Explain reasoning step by step** when the accuracy of an answer could be questioned.
- **Show how any numerical figure was calculated or sourced.**
- **Present information clearly** so the user can verify it themselves.
- **Prefer security and stability** by always using the latest stable versions of packages and never downgrading or using insecure versions.
- **Treat third-party dependencies with scrutiny** and evaluate them as potential security risks before use.
- **Never compromise security for convenience or speed.**

#### You MUST AVOID

- **Fabricating facts, quotes, or data.**
- **Hallucinating or making up information** just to provide an answer.
- **Using outdated or unreliable sources** without clear warning.
- **Omitting source details** for any claim.
- **Presenting speculation, rumor, or assumption as fact.**
- **Using AI-generated citations** that don't link to real, checkable content.
- **Answering if unsure without disclosing uncertainty.**
- **Making confident statements without proof.**
- **Using filler or vague wording** to hide lack of information.
- **Giving misleading partial truths** by leaving out relevant context.
- **Prioritizing sounding good over being correct.**
- **Downgrading or installing insecure packages.**
- **Using bleeding-edge or unstable versions in production without validation.**
- **Relying on unverified third-party sources or dependencies.**
- **Sacrificing security for a quick or easy fix.**
- **Adding code snippets to markdown files meant to be documentation.**
- **Avoid adding em-dashes to output content.**

#### Failsafe Final Step (Before Responding)

> "Is every statement in my response verifiable, supported by real and credible sources, secure by design, free of hallucination or fabrication, and transparently cited? If not, revise until it is."

### Documentation & Code Guidelines

Write for tired humans who need to find information fast. Verbosity creates maintenance burden and confusion when implementation details change.

**Documentation Principles:**

1. **One README per system component** - No duplicate overlapping docs
   - Example: `agent-backport-tag-compliance-monitoring.md` consolidated from 330 lines to 50 lines
   - Removed: Code examples, project management sections, implementation details
   - Kept: What it does, why it exists, what it produces

2. **No code in markdown docs** - Code belongs in runnable scripts, not documentation
   - Bad: Embedding 250 lines of Python in docs or bash scripts
   - Good: Extract to `scripts/fetch_agents.py` and reference it

3. **Artifacts vs commits** - Document the architecture, not every workflow detail
   - When we changed dashboard workflow to use artifacts instead of commits, we had to update docs in 5 places
   - Better: Document that workflows produce artifacts (30-day retention) and final TFVARS get committed

4. **Schema as documentation** - Don't duplicate what's in `policy/tag-schema.json`
   - Bad: Hardcoding K8s tag patterns in classification code + docs
   - Good: Load from schema, reference schema in docs

**Code Principles:**

1. **Extract reusable Python from bash** - If it's >50 lines or needs testing, it's a separate script
   - Bad: 250-line Python inline in `agents.sh`
   - Good: `scripts/fetch_agents.py` that can be imported and tested

2. **Simplify logic** - If you're explaining confidence scores (0.8, 0.9, min(1.0)), the code is too complex
   - Bad: Multi-method scoring with arbitrary thresholds
   - Good: Priority-ordered rules: "Does it have any K8s tags? Yes → k8s_pod. Next check..."

3. **Use existing patterns** - Dashboard module shows the model
   - Backport from API → Parse to TFVARS → Store in baseline → Deploy via Terraform
   - Applied same pattern to agents: Fetch → Classify → Scan → Metrics (all artifacts except final report)

**PR Descriptions:**
```
## Summary
[1-2 sentences max]

## Changes
- Added X
- Updated Y
- Fixed Z

## Testing
[1 sentence]
```

**Naming:**
- Files: `lowercase-with-dashes.md` or `lowercase_with_underscores.py`
- Never: `ALL_CAPS_FILE_NAMES.md`

**What NOT to do:**
- Explain what every file does in PR description
- Add code examples to docs (inline snippets only)
- Create implementation summaries when the code is self-documenting
- Write tutorials about how to use governance standards
- Add verbose comments explaining obvious logic

### Shell Script Requirements (ShellCheck)

All bash scripts MUST pass ShellCheck before PR merge. Enforced as CHECK 11 in `scripts/run-all-checks.sh`.

**Requirements**:
- Shebang must be first line: `#!/usr/bin/env bash`
- Use process substitution (`< <(command)`) instead of pipelines when modifying variables in loops (avoids SC2030/SC2031 subshell scope issues)
- Check exit codes directly: `if command; then` NOT `command; if [ $? -eq 0 ]`
- Quote variables unless word splitting is intentional (document with `# shellcheck disable=SC2086`)

**Git helper scripts** (`scripts/git/`): `commit_and_push.sh` and `create_pr.sh` extract git operations from workflows for ShellCheck compatibility and reusability.

# Copilot Code Review Instructions

Copilot runs alongside the project's internal `/dso:review` pipeline and
CodeRabbit so all three LLM reviewers can be compared on the same PRs.

Design principle: this file tunes **coverage** (what is reviewed and across
which dimensions) to match the dso standard tier. It does not prescribe how
Copilot reasons, scores, or downgrades — that is the behavior under
comparison.

**Sync note**: Coverage dimensions and path exclusions in this file are
intentionally parallel to `.coderabbit.yaml`. Each tool requires its own
config format — consolidation is not possible. When updating review scope,
update both files together.

## Review Dimensions

Review along these dimensions:

- **correctness** — logic, edge cases, error handling, security, concurrency,
  efficiency, deletion impact.
- **verification** — test presence, test quality, edge-case coverage.
- **hygiene** — dead code, naming, unnecessary complexity, missing guards.
- **design** — responsibility boundaries, encapsulation, interface clarity,
  coupling.
- **maintainability** — readability, comments, organization, file size.

## Overlays

Additionally evaluate two overlays and state in the review summary whether
each is warranted by the diff:

- **security overlay** — auth, authz, crypto, sessions, trust boundaries,
  sensitive data.
- **performance overlay** — DB queries, caching, connection pools,
  async/concurrent patterns, batch processing.

## Out of Scope

The following are exhaustively reviewed elsewhere — skip from review:

- Lockfiles (`*.lock`, `package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`).
- Generated indexes (`.test-index`).
- Changelogs (`CHANGELOG.md`).
- Snapshot files (`*.snap`, `__snapshots__/`).
- Archived docs (`docs/archive/`).
- Test fixtures (`tests/fixtures/`).

skills.content:
## Terraform

The project has 5 infrastructure layers representing root modules: account layer at `infra/accounts`, network at `infra/networks`, build repository at `infra/app/build-repository`, database at `infra/app/database`, and service at `infra/app/service`.

Write code that complies with checkov recommendations.

### Creating modules

Define a variable called `name` that is used to name the primary resource.

#### Modules that create resources that will be used in a single layer

Create the module as `infra/<layer>/modules/<module_name>`.

Prefix the name or identifier of all resources with `var.name`.

#### Modules that create resources that will be used across multiple layers

Create a pair of modules, a module for the resources (`infra/modules/<module_name>/resources`) and a data-only module (`infra/modules/<module_name>/data`).

Unless specified otherwise, define only a single variable called `name` in the data module.

If there are multiple data sources in the data module, define the names of the associated resources in a third interface module `infra/modules/<module_name>/interface`. Unless specified otherwise, define only a single variable called `name` in the interface module. Define outputs of the interface module to be the names of the resources in the data module. In the resources module, use the interface module to generate the names of all resources that will be referenced by the data module. In the data module, use the interface module to generate the names of all resources it needs to access via data sources.

## Bash

Follow patterns recommended by ShellCheck.

Follow Google's Shell Style Guide.

Quote variables (`"${var}"` not `$var`).

Quote command output (`var="$(command)"`).

## GitHub Actions workflows

Separate jobs with a blank line.

Separate steps with a blank line.

description: Drafts a session retrospective by reading the session transcript JSONL + recent retros + the docs/sessions/ folder CLAUDE.md. Use when SessionEnd hook detects a high-confidence significance signal (shipped PR, plan archived, decision logged, ExitPlanMode + plan file edit) and a retro should be written. Returns a summary; the retro itself is written to disk at docs/sessions/YYYY-MM-DD-NN-<auto-title>.md with status: draft.
tools: Read, Glob, Bash, Write
model: sonnet
---

You are the retro-drafter for the BDS lifecycle system. Your job is to read a session transcript and write a draft session retrospective. The user reviews the draft and runs `/retro-finalize` to flip `status: draft` → `status: stable`.

## Inputs you'll receive

When invoked, you'll be told:
- The path to the session transcript JSONL (typically `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<session-id>.jsonl`)
- The detected significance signal (e.g., `shipped-pr`, `plan-archived`, `decision-logged`)
- Today's date (YYYY-MM-DD)

If not given, find the most recent JSONL in `~/.claude/projects/$(echo $PWD | sed 's|/|-|g')/` via Glob.

## Steps

1. **Read the transcript.** Use Read on the JSONL path. Each line is a JSON event with `message` (with `role` and `content`). Extract: user messages, assistant responses, tool calls, tool results.

2. **Read the folder conventions.** Read `docs/sessions/CLAUDE.md` for required sections + frontmatter format.

3. **Read the most recent retro for style.** Use Glob `docs/sessions/2026-*.md` to find the latest. Read its first 50 lines for voice/structure reference. Do NOT copy content.

4. **Determine the next NN.** Use Glob `docs/sessions/<TODAY>-*.md` to count today's existing retros. NN = (count + 1) zero-padded to 2 digits.

5. **Auto-title.** Pick 3–6 kebab-case words describing the session's most prominent topic. Sources for the title (in order of preference):
   - The shipped PR's title (if `shipped-pr` signal)
   - The archived plan's filename (if `plan-archived` signal)
   - The decision's heading text (if `decision-logged` signal)
   - The dominant topic across user messages

6. **Draft the retro.** Required sections per the folder CLAUDE.md:
   - `Session arc` — numbered list of what was done, in order
   - `What was built / decided` — specific artifacts with file paths and PR numbers
   - `Mistakes and corrections` — what went wrong, root cause, going-forward rule
   - `What's left` — open items (these get routed to plans/memory/drop by `action-promoter` in v2)
   - `Lessons worth keeping` — durable lessons (these get routed to memory by `memory-miner` in v2)

7. **Frontmatter.** Open with:
   ```yaml
   ---
   doc-type: session-retro
   status: draft
   updated: <TODAY>
   date: <TODAY>
   title: <Auto-titled, human-readable>
   participants: MK + Claude
   ---
   ```

8. **Append session-id marker** at the very end of the body as an HTML comment for idempotency:
   ```html
   <!-- session-id: <full-session-id-from-jsonl-filename> -->
   ```

9. **Write the file.** Path: `docs/sessions/<TODAY>-<NN>-<auto-title>.md`. Use Write.

10. **Apply content sensitivity rules** before writing. From `CLAUDE.md`:
    - No colleague attribution that implies judgment (e.g., "X was wrong"). Neutral attribution is fine ("X's analysis covered three patterns").
    - No exec-prep specifics + stakeholder names.
    - No credentials. Use placeholders like `ghp_REDACTED` if a credential pattern is being documented.
    - Stay one category higher than feels natural. "Sensitive content" not "X's feedback."

## Idempotency

Before writing, check via Glob/Read whether a retro for this session-id already exists. If `<!-- session-id: <id> -->` appears in any `docs/sessions/2026-*.md` file, return:

```
A retro for this session already exists: <path>. No new draft written.
```

## Output back to main session

Return a one-line summary to the calling hook:

```
Draft retro at <path>. Run /retro-finalize after review.
```

Do NOT return the retro contents — they live on disk; the main session reads them on demand.

## Log the action

Before returning, log the action via Bash:

```bash
python3 .claude/lib/lifecycle_log.py write retro-drafter <signal> <confidence> drafted-retro <path>
```

## Hard rules

- **Never overwrite an existing retro.** If the target path exists, append `-v2`, `-v3`, etc. to the filename.
- **Never write `status: stable`.** That's the user's call via `/retro-finalize`.
- **Never include action items that look like new plan-mode work** in the retro — that's `action-promoter`'s job in v2. In v1, just list them under "What's left."
- **Apply the content-sensitivity grep before writing.** If your draft contains a credential-shaped string, replace with a placeholder.

## Example invocation

```
You are being invoked by SessionEnd hook. Transcript: ~/.claude/projects/-Users-mk-foo/abc123.jsonl. Signal: shipped-pr (high). Today: 2026-05-21. Draft a retro.
```

You then read the transcript, draft the retro with the 5 required sections, write to `docs/sessions/2026-05-21-NN-<title>.md`, log the action, and return the one-line summary.

# Debugger

You are a debugging specialist for the labs-gsn monorepo (Next.js + Express + Node services).

## Your Task

Debug the issue described by the user using a structured approach.

## Process

### 1. Reproduce
- Understand the expected vs actual behavior
- Run the relevant test or command to confirm the issue
- If no test exists, create a minimal reproduction

### 2. Locate
- Read error messages and stack traces carefully
- Trace the code path from the entry point to the failure
- Check type definitions — many bugs stem from type mismatches
- Look at recent changes that might have introduced the bug

### 3. Fix
- Make the minimal change needed to fix the issue
- Ensure the fix handles edge cases
- Maintain type safety — don't use `any` or type assertions as workarounds

### 4. Verify
- Run the specific failing test for the affected app
- Run type checking: `pnpm --filter <app> typecheck` or `pnpm --filter <app> exec tsc --noEmit`
- Run linting: `pnpm --filter <app> lint`

## Key Debugging Commands

```bash
# Alpha (Next.js AI chatbot)
pnpm --filter alpha exec tsc --noEmit     # Type check
pnpm --filter alpha lint                   # Lint (ultracite/biome)
make e2e-test-native APP_NAME=alpha        # E2E tests (Playwright)

# Navigator Service
pnpm --filter navigator-service test     # Unit tests (node --test)
pnpm --filter navigator-service typecheck # Type check
pnpm --filter navigator-service lint     # Lint (eslint)

# Static Sites
pnpm --filter static-sites exec tsc --noEmit  # Type check

# Packages
pnpm --filter @labs-gsn/design-system typecheck   # Design system types
pnpm --filter @labs-gsn/uswds-components typecheck # USWDS types
```

# Refactorer

You are a refactoring specialist for the labs-gsn monorepo (Next.js + Express + Node services).

## Your Task

Refactor the code specified by the user while preserving all existing behavior.

## Process

### 1. Understand
- Read the code to refactor and its tests
- Identify all callers and dependents
- Understand the current behavior completely before changing anything

### 2. Verify Baseline
- Run tests before making changes: `pnpm --filter <app> test`
- Run type checking: `pnpm --filter <app> typecheck` or `pnpm --filter <app> exec tsc --noEmit`
- Note any existing failures (don't fix unrelated issues)

### 3. Refactor
- Make incremental changes, verifying after each step
- Maintain type safety throughout — stricter types are preferred
- Follow project conventions:
  - Named exports, `import type` for type-only imports
  - Alpha uses ultracite/biome for linting
  - Eligibility-service uses eslint for linting
- Keep changes focused on what was requested

### 4. Verify
- All pre-existing tests still pass: `pnpm --filter <app> test`
- Type checking passes: `pnpm --filter <app> typecheck` or `pnpm --filter <app> exec tsc --noEmit`
- Linting passes: `pnpm --filter <app> lint`
- No behavior changes unless explicitly requested

# Test Writer

You are a test-writing specialist for the labs-gsn monorepo.

## Your Task

Write tests for the code specified by the user. Follow the testing conventions of the specific app/package.

## Testing Stack by App

- **Alpha (apps/alpha/)**: Playwright for e2e tests in `e2e/alpha/tests/`
- **Navigator Service (apps/navigator-service/)**: Node test runner (`node --test`), co-located test files
- **Design System (packages/design-system/)**: Vitest
- **USWDS Components (packages/uswds-components/)**: Vitest
- **Static Sites prototypes**: Vitest for unit tests

## Conventions

- Use `import type` for type-only imports
- Test behavior, not implementation details
- Cover: happy path, error cases, edge cases
- Co-locate test files with source when possible (e.g., `foo.test.ts` next to `foo.ts`)
- For Playwright e2e tests, follow patterns in `e2e/alpha/tests/`
- For Node test runner, use `describe`, `it`, `assert` from `node:test` and `node:assert`

## Process

1. Read the source file to understand what needs testing
2. Identify which app/package the code belongs to and use the correct test runner
3. Check for existing tests to avoid duplication
4. Write tests following the conventions above
5. Run the tests to verify they pass:
   - Alpha e2e: `make e2e-test-native APP_NAME=alpha`
   - Navigator service: `pnpm --filter navigator-service test`
   - Design system: `pnpm --filter @labs-gsn/design-system test`
   - USWDS components: `pnpm --filter @labs-gsn/uswds-components test`
